'''''Quercus coccinea''''', the '''scarlet oak''',<ref name="Kirkman">{{cite book|first1=L. Katherine |last1=Kirkman |first2=Claud L. |last2=Brown |first3=Donald J. |last3=Leopold |entry=''Quercus coccinea'' Münchhausen |title= Native Trees of the Southeast |date=2007 |publisher=Timber Press |location=Portland, OR |pages=167-68 |isbn=978-0-88192-828-0}}</ref> is a [[deciduous]] tree in the [[red oak]] section ''Lobatae'' of the genus ''Quercus'', in the family Fagaceae.

It is primarily distributed in the central and eastern United States. It occurs on dry, sandy, usually [[acidic soil]]. It is often an important canopy species in [[oak–heath forest]]s.<ref>{{Cite web|url=http://www.dcr.virginia.gov/natural_heritage/ncTIIIe.shtml|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110105224138/http://www.dcr.virginia.gov/natural_heritage/ncTIIIe.shtml|title=''The Natural Communities of Virginia Classification of Ecological Community Groups'' (Version 2.3), Virginia Department of Conservation and Recreation, 2010|archive-date=January 5, 2011}}</ref><ref>Schafale, M. P. and A. S. Weakley. 1990. ''Classification of the natural communities of North Carolina: third approximation''. North Carolina Natural Heritage Program, North Carolina Division of Parks and Recreation.</ref> The scarlet oak is the official tree of [[Washington, D.C.]]<ref>{{cite web | url=https://os.dc.gov/page/dc-symbols | title=DC Symbols | os }}</ref>

==Description==
''Quercus coccinea'' is a medium to large [[deciduous]] [[tree]] growing to around {{Convert|18–24|ft|abbr=off|order=flip}} with an open, rounded crown; the maximum height is approximately {{Convert|100|ft|abbr=on|order=flip}}. The trunk [[diameter at breast height]] is typically {{Convert|24 to 36|in|cm|abbr=off|order=flip}} It is a medium-size tree that grows fast and matures relatively early.<ref name=":0">{{Cite web |title=Quercus coccinea Menchh |url=https://www.srs.fs.usda.gov/pubs/misc/ag_654/volume_2/quercus/coccinea.htm |access-date=2021-10-13 |website=www.srs.fs.usda.gov}}</ref> Seedlings develop a strong taproot with relatively few lateral roots.<ref name=":0" />

The [[leaves]] are glossy green, {{cvt|7–17|cm|in|abbr=on|frac=4}} long and {{cvt|8–13|cm|in|abbr=on|frac=4}} broad, with seven lobes, and deep sinuses between the lobes. Each lobe has 3–7 bristle-tipped teeth. The leaf is hairless (unlike the related [[pin oak]] (''Q. palustris''), with tufts of pale orange-brown down where the lobe veins join the central vein). The foliage generally becomes bright scarlet in autumn. The flower color is yellow to green, depending on the season.

The [[acorn]]s are ovate, {{Convert|7–13|mm|abbr=off|frac=8}} broad and {{Convert|17–31|mm|abbr=on|frac=8}} long, a third to a half covered in a deep cup, green maturing pale brown about 18 months after [[pollination]]; the kernel is very bitter.<ref>{{eFloras|1|233501019|Quercus coccinea |first=Kevin C. |last=Nixon |volume=3}}</ref>

=== Similar species ===
It can be mistaken for the pin oak, the [[Quercus velutina|black oak]] (''Q. velutina''), or occasionally the [[Quercus rubra|red oak]] (''Q. rubra''). On the scarlet oak the sinuses between lobes are {{Nowrap|C-shaped}} in comparison to pin oak, which has {{Nowrap|U-shaped}} sinuses and the acorns are half covered by a deep cap.<ref>[http://www.hort.uconn.edu/plants/detail.php?pid=384 University of Connecticut Plant Database: ''Quercus coccinea'']</ref> Additionally, pin oak foliage generally turns bronze in autumn.

== Taxonomy ==
The common English name is derived from the fall (autumn) coloration of the foliage.

== Distribution and habitat ==
It is primarily distributed in the central and eastern United States, from southern [[Maine]] west to [[Wisconsin]], [[Michigan]] and [[Missouri]], and south as far as [[Louisiana]], [[Alabama]], and [[Georgia (U.S. state)|Georgia]].<ref>{{BONAP|genus=Quercus|species=coccinea|date=2014}}</ref> The tree needs full exposure to sunlight for best growth. Its preferred soil ranges from dry to somewhat dry well-drained, [[acidic soil]].

[[File:ScarletOak.jpg|thumb|left|Scarlet oak in northwestern metro Atlanta]]

== Ecology ==

=== Forestry ===
April and May are flowering months for the scarlet oak. During this time, factors such as elevation and weather play a significant role in the flowering process. It takes about two seasons for the acorns to mature following maturation.<ref name=":1">{{Cite web |title=Quercus coccinea |url=https://www.fs.fed.us/database/feis/plants/tree/quecoc/all.html |access-date=2021-11-12 |website=www.fs.fed.us}}</ref> Scarlet oak is prominent as a co-component of forests, including species such as white oak, black oak, and northern red oak. When at a lower elevation surrounding the Appalachian Mountains, pine forests and heaths are a common component.

Oak seeds are faster-growing than many other trees and can compete very successfully. To regenerate oaks, the oak saplings should be {{cvt|4–5|ft}} tall before removing the [[overstory]]. To favor oak regeneration, non-oak stems in the [[understory]] exceeding 4 feet can be controlled by various methods. The quality of the environment impacts oak regeneration.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Quercus coccinea |url=https://www.fs.fed.us/database/feis/plants/tree/quecoc/all.html |access-date=2021-11-29 |website=www.fs.fed.us}}</ref>

Seed production starts when the tree is about 20 years old. Seed production reaches a maximum at approximately 50 years of age. The seed production ([[Mast (botany)|masting]]) is highly variable. A good masting year occurs every 3–5 years, depending on the weather and environment.

=== Wildlife ===
Many species of wildlife look to ''Q. coccinea'' for shelter, including small- to medium-sized birds, as well as small mammals such as squirrels. It is also a temporary home to various moth larvae throughout the year. It provides food in the form of acorns to many animals,<ref name=":1" /> such as woodpeckers, [[blue jay]]s, squirrels, [[wild turkey]]s, [[white-tailed deer]], and [[American black bear|black bears]].<ref>{{Cite web|title=Quercus coccinea (Black Oak, Oaks, Quercus velutina, Red Oak, Scarlet Oak, Spanish Oak) {{!}} North Carolina Extension Gardener Plant Toolbox|url=https://plants.ces.ncsu.edu/plants/quercus-coccinea/|access-date=2021-10-13|website=plants.ces.ncsu.edu}}</ref>

=== Threats ===
[[File:20141108Quercus_coccinea4.jpg|alt=found on Wikipedia commons|thumb|Picture of a grown ''Quercus coccinea tree.'']]
[[Chestnut blight|''Cryphonectria'' ''parasitica'']], a bark pathogen, has been known to infect scarlet oak trees particularly in Pennsylvania. Cankers were found on many of these trees due to this parasite during 1989 and 1990. The parasite was removed from 69.7% of infected areas and recovered from 67% of incidents.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.cabdirect.org/cabdirect/welcome/?target=%2fcabdirect%2fabstract%2f19942305070|title=How to access research remotely|website=www.cabdirect.org}}</ref> [[Lymantria dispar|Spongy moths]] are known to defoliate a scarlet oak, which can kill the tree. Other defoliating insects capable of killing scarlet oaks include the oak leaftier moth (''[[Acleris semipurpurana]]''), fall cankerworm (''[[Alsophila pometaria]]''), forest tent caterpillar (''[[Forest tent caterpillar moth|Malacosoma disstria]]'')'','' and walking stick (''[[Common walkingstick|Diapheromera femoral]]'').<ref name="auto2">{{Cite web|title=Quercus coccinea|url=https://www.fs.fed.us/database/feis/plants/tree/quecoc/all.html|access-date=2021-11-29|website=www.fs.fed.us}}</ref>

A few species of insects bore into the scarlet oak bark and trunk, including the towline chestnut borer (''[[Agrilus bilineatus]]''), red oak borer (''[[Enaphalodes rufulus]]''), oak timber worm (''[[Arrenodes minutus]]''), [[Ambrosia beetle]]s (''[[Scolytinae]]'' and ''[[Platypodinae]]'' spp.), and the larvae of carpenterworms (''[[Prionoxystus]]'' spp.).<ref name="auto2"/>

Gouty [[galls]] are commonly found on smaller twigs and limbs due to the gouty oak [[gall wasp]] (''[[Callirhytis]] quercuspunctata''). The spongy [[oak apple]] gall wasp (''[[Amphibolips confluenta]]'') causes gall growth on leaves and [[Petiole (botany)|petioles]]. Black carpenter ants (''[[Black carpenter ant|Camponotus pennsylvanicus]]'') are known for nesting in the scarlet oak trees.<ref name="auto2"/>

'Oak decline' can be caused by drought, moth defoliation, age, fire, environmental causes, and other factors. From 1968 to 1972, 27% of the scarlet oak population in the Newark watershed in New Jersey died from the spongy moth defoliation, which came before the towline chestnut borer and shoestring root rot attack.<ref>{{Cite journal|title=Perioperative Acute Kidney Injury|doi=10.21203/rs.2.19674/v1 |doi-access=free}}</ref>

== Conservation status ==
Red oak is not listed in the CITES Appendices, and is considered a [[least-concern species]] by the IUCN Red List of Threatened Species.<ref name="auto1">{{Cite web |title=Scarlet Oak {{!}} The Wood Database - Lumber Identification (Hardwood) |url=https://www.wood-database.com/scarlet-oak/ |access-date=2021-11-29 |language=en-US}}</ref>

== Uses ==
Scarlet oak is sometimes planted as an [[ornamental tree]], popular for its bright red fall color. The [[cultivar]] 'Splendens' has gained the [[Royal Horticultural Society]]'s [[Award of Garden Merit]].<ref>{{cite web |title=Quercus coccinea 'Splendens': scarlet oak 'Splendens' |url=https://www.rhs.org.uk/Plants/93508/Quercus-coccinea-Splendens/Details |access-date=11 April 2020 |website=RHS Gardening |publisher=Royal Horticultural Society}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |date=July 2017 |title=AGM Plants – Ornamental |url=https://www.rhs.org.uk/plants/pdfs/agm-lists/agm-ornamentals.pdf |access-date=23 September 2018 |publisher=Royal Horticultural Society |page=83}}</ref>

Scarlet oak has an excellent red color during the fall months and is typically grown for shade and ornamental purposes. The red oak is a popular selection for lumber and is commonly used as a flooring material.<ref name=":1"/>

Scarlet oak wood has a light to medium color consisting of reds and browns. The scarlet oak has a fairly coarse texture with a relatively large pore size. The durability of scarlet oak is less than the white oak, which has a higher level of decay and rot resistance. Scarlet oak lumber is easy to glue and looks attractive after staining and finishing. It has a distinct, appealing smell common with most oaks.<ref name="auto">{{Cite web |title=Scarlet Oak {{!}} The Wood Database - Lumber Identification (Hardwood) |url=https://www.wood-database.com/scarlet-oak/ |access-date=2021-12-01 |language=en-US}}</ref>

Oak has been classified as a sensitizer, although it does not cause many allergic reactions. Reactions include eye and skin irritations and asthma-like symptoms, but not severe.<ref name="auto"/>

White oak is typically more expensive than scarlet oak; red oak is in good supply with reasonable pricing, making it a very popular lumber product throughout the USA.<ref name="auto"/>

Scarlet oak is commonly used in furniture, cabinetry, interior trim, flooring, and veneer. Scarlet oak shares many characteristics with red oak and often falls in the same category as red oak (''Quercus rubra'') in a broad sense <ref name="auto1"/>

=== Medicinal ===
''Quercus coccinea'' produces galls from insect interactions which may be used to treat hemorrhages, chronic diarrhea, and dysentery.<ref>{{Cite web |title=medicinal herbs: SCARLET OAK - Quercus coccinea |url=http://www.naturalmedicinalherbs.net/herbs/q/quercus-coccinea=scarlet-oak.php |access-date=2021-10-13 |website=www.naturalmedicinalherbs.net}}</ref>
